name: Generalized Eruptive Histiocytosis

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical and Histopathological Diagnostic Criteria for Generalized Eruptive Histiocytosis

criteria.description: Multiple widespread erythematous to brown papules and nodules appearing in crops
Skin biopsy showing dermal infiltrate of non-Langerhans cell histiocytes without Birbeck granules
Positive staining for CD68 and factor XIIIa, negative for CD1a and S100
No evidence of Langerhans cell histiocytosis clinically or histologically
Exclusion of infectious, malignant, or other histiocytic disorders

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of characteristic clinical lesions plus histopathological confirmation with appropriate immunohistochemical profile
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis relies heavily on skin biopsy and immunohistochemical staining to differentiate from other histiocytoses

occasional.symptomName: Increased serum mast cell beta-tryptase concentration

laboratory: Normal blood counts in most cases
Occasional mild elevation of inflammatory markers
imaging: Usually normal; imaging may be used to exclude systemic involvement
genetic: No known specific genetic mutations associated
other: Skin biopsy with characteristic histiocytic infiltrate
Immunohistochemistry positive for CD68 and factor XIIIa, negative for CD1a and S100

distinguishingFeatures: Presence of Birbeck granules on electron microscopy
Often systemic involvement with bone lesions
Typically affects infants and young children
Lesions are yellow plaques rather than papules

redFlags: Rapid progression of skin lesions with ulceration
Development of systemic symptoms such as fever or weight loss
Neurological deficits indicating possible CNS involvement
references: Fraitag S, et al. Generalized eruptive histiocytosis: clinical and histopathological features. J Am Acad Dermatol. 2015.
Orphanet Report: Generalized Eruptive Histiocytosis. Orphanet 2023.
Weitzman S, et al. Histiocytic disorders of childhood. Blood. 2005.
